item.title: Artificial Intelligence, Future Skills, and Productivity
item.content:encoded:
Tony Fang, Memorial University

Jennifer A. Harrison, EM Normandie Business School

Artificial intelligence is reshaping organizations by reconfiguring task structures, skill requirements, and managerial processes. Rather than eliminating jobs, AI adoption fosters new occupational roles and redefines expertise through changed patterns of human-AI collaboration. These developments promise to enhance productivity, though realizing these gains depends critically on the human skills that enable effective technology use.

The concept of skills varies significantly across disciplines, from labour economics viewing skills as human capital to organizational psychology emphasizing cognitive capabilities and sociology examining how skills are socially constructed. This fragmented understanding limits integrated knowledge about how AI shapes skills and productivity. The call seeks to bridge these perspectives by examining how skills are identified, defined, and valued in relation to AI, and how they translate into productivity gains across contexts.

Appel publié par Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences / Revue Canadienne des Sciences de l Administration. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • AI adoption and implementation in organizations, including how skills are identified, defined, measured, valued, and linked to productivity
  • Human and AI collaboration, work transformation, and the identification and use of skills in changing task contexts
  • Defining and developing skills in workplaces using AI (e.g., reskilling, upskilling, lifelong learning) and linking to productivity
  • Changes in occupations, expertise, and professional roles, and how skill requirements are defined and evolving with AI
  • Organizational and institutional factors shaping how skills are identified, defined, and managed in relation to AI and productivity (e.g., leadership, HR practices, policy contexts)
  • Career sustainability, mobility, and inequality in labour markets shaped by AI, with a focus on how skills are defined, accessed, and valued

Timeline

  • December 15, 2026: Submission Deadline

item.title: Blockchain-Based Operating Systems and the Application of AI-Enabled Complexity Management in Organizations
item.content:encoded:
Ilan Alon, Ariel University

Marcin Wątorek, Cracow University of Technology

Aušrinė Šilenskytė, University of Vaasa

Ziaul Haque Munim, University of South-Eastern Norway

Organizations increasingly manage distributed decision-making and systemic complexity through blockchain technologies that function as operating systems by embedding governance mechanisms into digital infrastructures. These systems are being advanced with artificial intelligence to monitor and shape behavior. Despite blockchain-based operating systems being adopted in platforms, supply chains, and decentralized autonomous organizations, their implications for organizational administration, governance, and control remain poorly understood.

This special issue invites research that advances administrative and organizational understanding of blockchain-based operating systems with AI-enabled complexity. The call welcomes theoretically grounded, methodologically rigorous contributions including empirical studies and theory-building papers that offer clear organizational insights and engage meaningfully with blockchain and AI as organizational infrastructures.

Appel publié par Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences / Revue Canadienne des Sciences de l Administration. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Blockchain as an organizational operating system and potential of AI advancements in it
  • Public, private, and hybrid organizations adopting blockchain OS with AI advancements
  • Integration of AI on Blockchain OS in crowdsourcing platforms, crypto exchanges, fintech firms, energy management, and transport services etc.
  • Organizational decision-making in blockchain-based and AI enabled systems
  • AI's role in administrative functions embedded in smart contracts and protocols
  • Token-based incentives as administrative and managerial mechanisms
  • Strategic control and accountability in decentralized platforms with AI-enabled advancements
  • AI integration in governance, coordination, and control without centralized authority (DAOs)
  • Complexity, emergence, and adaptation in blockchain-based and AI enabled organizations
  • Organizational legitimacy, regulation, and institutional alignment in AI and blockchain OS integrations
  • Ethical, responsible, and sustainable administration of blockchain systems, especially those advanced with AI

Timeline

  • November 15, 2026: Submission Deadline

item.title: Governing the Ungovernable? Corporate accountability, board roles, and organizational responsibility in the age of (artificial) intelligence
item.content:encoded:
Kim Ceulemans, TBS Business School

Lotfi Karoui, ISC Paris

Agota Szabo, VU Amsterdam

Wafa Khlif, TBS Business School

Organizations increasingly rely on AI for consequential decisions across hiring, credit, and compliance. Yet governance frameworks designed for human-centered processes struggle to address distributed, opaque systems operating at unprecedented scale and speed. Traditional oversight mechanisms—boards, audit committees, regulators—were not built to govern technologies that challenge assumptions about accountability and responsibility.

This special issue examines how corporate governance frameworks can evolve to address AI's organizational implications. Rather than treating governance as purely technical, the issue emphasizes that governance shapes whose interests matter and how accountability is defined. The call seeks research exploring the mismatch between rapid, complex AI-enabled decision-making and slower institutional oversight.

Appel publié par Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences / Revue Canadienne des Sciences de l Administration. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Board oversight of AI, algorithmic risk, and digital infrastructures
  • Fiduciary duty, corporate purpose, and stakeholder accountability in AI-intensive firms
  • AI, sustainability, and the governance of social and environmental impacts
  • Algorithmic management, the organization of labour, and workplace surveillance
  • Audit, assurance, internal control, and the challenge of model opacity
  • AI regulation, soft law, and the organizational translation of legal requirements
  • Data governance, data ownership, and cross-border accountability
  • Bias, discrimination, and issues related to classification, prediction, and fairness in AI systems
  • Human oversight, contestability, and the limits of explainability
  • AI in public administration, welfare systems, healthcare, policing, and education
  • The role of AI in sensitive or high-impact contexts, including security, defense, and critical infrastructures
  • Alternative and plural governance models for responsible AI
  • Stakeholder participation, oversight, and engagement in AI governance

Timeline

  • December 25, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Phygital Leadership for Human-Centric Business Models and Enhanced Innovation, and Operational Delivery
item.content:encoded:
Wided Batat, University of Lyon 2

Boris Bartikowski, Kedge Business School

Zhiyong Yang, Miami University

Kelley Cours Anderson, College of Charleston

Contemporary organizations navigate hybrid work cultures and digital transformation, yet many firms—especially micro enterprises and family businesses—remain in closed ecosystems lacking phygital integration. This special issue explores how phygital leadership, which seamlessly merges physical and digital workplaces, can be adapted across diverse organizational contexts.

Phygital leadership represents a human-first framework emphasizing integration of digital and physical environments. The Phygital Research Paradigm proposes that successful transformation requires identifying enablers such as human capabilities, technological platforms, and material supports to achieve value through seamless transitions between physical and digital modes.

The special issue invites scholars and practitioners to explore phygital leadership's strategic significance and implementation pathways for developing human-centric business models suited to hybrid work cultures, addressing gaps in narrowly focused digital leadership research.

Appel publié par Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences / Revue Canadienne des Sciences de l Administration. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Evolution of leadership styles in phygital environments
  • Human-centric organizational innovation in the phygital ecosystem
  • Dual-plane leadership transformation: physicalization vs. digitalization
  • Ethical design and responsible phygital practices
  • Stakeholder engagement and phygital value co-creation
  • Phygital leadership-driven well-being and social impact
  • Phygital workplace culture, equity, and inclusivity
  • Technology-human interaction in phygital leadership models
  • Strategic implementation and scaling of phygital leadership
  • Cognitive and emotional labor of phygital leaders
  • The role of data-driven systems and AI tools co-construct leadership decision-making
  • Rethinking contemporary competency models for phygital leadership

  • Phygital leadership as a strategic capability in digital transformation

item.title: The Challenges of Social Media Influencers: AI Integration, Strategic Agency, and New Business Models in Global-Local Digital Markets
item.content:encoded:
Raffaele Filieri, Audencia Business School

Elmira Djafarova, Northumbria University

Margot Racat, IDRAC Business School

Veronika Keller, Szechenyi Istvan University

Rickard Enstroem, MacEwan University

Social media influencer marketing faces uncertainty amid algorithm fatigue, regulatory scrutiny, declining consumer trust, and AI-generated influencers. Traditional theoretical frameworks struggle to explain how AI content, algorithmic curation, and synthetic personas reshape influence dynamics.

This special issue examines whether traditional influencer marketing is ending or undergoing paradigm shift in how influence is constructed, monetized, and governed. It explores how authenticity, artificial intelligence, and algorithmic mediation intersect to reshape influence practices while addressing emerging regulatory frameworks.

The issue welcomes empirically grounded contributions from multiple disciplines including strategy, media studies, consumer behavior, and technology management. It particularly encourages interdisciplinary, globally inclusive research examining non-Western contexts, emerging platforms, and underrepresented influencer communities.

Appel publié par Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences / Revue Canadienne des Sciences de l Administration. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Trust, credibility, and authenticity in digital influence
  • Algorithmic mediation, platform governance, and market structure
  • Consumer resistance, fatigue, and agency
  • Virtual influencers, AI, and synthetic content
  • Cultural, generational, and global perspectives on influence
  • Professionalization, labor, and monetization in the creator economy
  • Ethics, power, and the dark side of influencer marketing
  • Expanding contexts of influence in B2B, nonprofit, and public sectors
  • Strategic navigation of platforms, algorithms, and AI tools across global-local digital markets
  • Authenticity and trust negotiation in activism, sustainability, and cause-related marketing
